lesson.menu_title: The Negotiation Room — Salary, Title and Scope
lesson.menu_desc: Asking about the range before you name a number, and attaching the condition to the yes -- 30 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 13 -- The Negotiation Room
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Fernando Meneghelli Bottura | Lesson 13 -- The Negotiation Room
lesson.grammar_point: would and could for hypothetical negotiation

listenings.text: Almost nobody loses money because they asked for too much. They lose it in two other ways. The first is naming a number before they know the range, because once it is out of your mouth it is a ceiling, and no client has ever offered me more than the candidate asked for. The second is making it personal. When a candidate tells me he needs more because of his mortgage, I have nothing to take to the client. When he tells me the scope grew by a shared service centre, I have a case, and I can argue it in a meeting he is not in. So ask what the range is, give me a reason that lives in the job and not in your life, and let me do the work. And say your number as a region, not as a demand.

The base was fixed and I knew it, so I stopped asking. What I negotiated instead was the reporting line, and I would do the same again. I asked for the finance function to report to the board rather than through the chief operating officer, and I asked for that in the contract, not in the conversation. It cost them nothing and it changed everything about the job. The second thing I asked for was a review of the scope at six months, in writing, because scope creep is the thing that makes people leave inside two years. The money in that offer was the same money. The job was a different job. If somebody tells you the number is final, that is often true, and it is also the moment the rest becomes negotiable.

extra_audio.text: Claire calls with an offer in the middle of the signed-off range. Fernando asks what range the role was signed off at, before naming anything. He asks for the upper half, with the scope as the reason. Claire asks what happens if the client holds the number. He says yes anyway, provided two things go into the contract.
